antworten: It defends the knight on c6 a second time.
It puts the question to the bishop on b5 at once: White must trade or retreat.
It prepares queenside castling.
fragen.erklaerung: The pawn on a6 attacks the bishop. In the main line, White retreats to a4 and keeps the pressure on c6.

unterschrift.text: , often called the “Berlin Wall”. The queens have been traded, and the black king has lost the right to castle. Black does have doubled pawns (two pawns on the same file) on c7 and c6 (gray squares), but in return has the bishop pair and no weakness through which White's pieces could quickly break in. That is why the position is considered extremely solid.

fragen.frage: Why is the Berlin endgame considered very solid for Black despite the doubled pawn?
antworten: Black has an extra pawn.
Black has the bishop pair and no weakness through which White can quickly break in.
The black king can still castle.
fragen.erklaerung: Material is level. The doubled pawn on c7/c6 is a drawback; the bishop pair and the lack of weaknesses make up for it.

Knights on c6 and f6, bishop on d7; the bishop from f8 was traded. The rooks are connected.
Castled, pawn shield untouched.
Castled, pawn shield untouched.
Conclusion:

The London System meets the three goals reliably and without risk, which is why it is so popular with beginners. The downside shows as well: White hardly exerts any pressure, and Black has also reached the goals without effort. If you want to win with the London System, you have to do it in the middlegame. The typical plan is the central advance
e4
, which Chapter 5 (Section 5.6) shows in this position.

Knight on c6, bishops on d6 and e6; the knight from f6 was traded.

Castled, pawn shield untouched.
Conclusion:
After ten moves, both sides have reached all three goals (
). The trade on move three shapes the whole position: White plays against the doubled pawns and the pawn on d5, Black wants to open the position for the bishop pair.
The chain d4–e5 stands and gains space.
The pawn on d5, supported by e6; both knights attack d4.

Conclusion:
After 13 moves, both sides have reached all three goals (
). The interim position after move eight (

The bishop on d7, however, remains the most passive piece on the board. Bringing it into play sensibly is the task for the middlegame.
The chain d4–e5 stands and gains space.

Conclusion:
After eleven moves, both sides have reached all three goals (
), two moves earlier than in the French Defense. The reason is the early bishop move to f5: Black no longer has a problem child to look after.

Conclusion:
After 15 moves, both sides have reached all three goals (

Conclusion:
After 17 moves, both sides have reached all three goals (
), much later than in the quiet openings. The interim position after ten moves (

Conclusion:

The Bishop's Opening leads to quiet positions in which both sides reach their goals without effort. Black even has a bit more of the center. This fits the description “flexible and solid”: White risks little, but also exerts little pressure.
The pawn on d4, isolated, but defended by the knight on f3 and the rook on d1.

Conclusion:
After twelve moves, both sides have reached all three goals (

). The fight for the center has turned into a fight over the isolated pawn on d4: White has active pieces and open lines in return, Black blockades the square d5 and waits for the endgame, in which the pawn becomes weak.
